query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single intervention of pre-coating tungsten (W) particles with a thin, uniform copper (Cu) layer by vapor deposition (e.g., CVD or PVD) before consolidation will promote superior interfacial bonding, reduce void formation and phase separation, and thus improve the thermal transport and mechanical durability of W–Cu composites under fusion‐reactor irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or interconnected W regions embedded in a conventional Cu matrix that may exhibit voids and compositional inhomogeneity from typical powder filling or direct sintering approaches.
generation.intervention: Apply a vapor deposition process to uniformly coat W particle surfaces with a thin layer of Cu prior to consolidation (e.g., spark plasma sintering).
generation.conditions: The vapor coating is done under conditions that avoid Cu melting (or significant diffusion) during deposition; subsequent consolidation is performed at temperatures below the melting point of Cu, with final testing under high thermal loads and irradiation representative of fusion reactor service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal and continuous Cu layer on W surfaces which minimizes interfacial voids and enhances wettability during sintering.
generation.mechanism: The vapor-deposited Cu layer cleans and passivates the W surface and provides a pre-established, highly uniform interface. During SPS consolidation, this layer promotes enhanced diffusion and interfacial bonding between W and Cu while suppressing phase separation and void formation that typically arise from mismatched processing dynamics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventional W–Cu composite (e.g., one made by direct filling or mechanical alloying without vapor pre-coating), the vapor-coated variant is expected to exhibit a more homogeneous microstructure with lower porosity, leading to improved thermal conductivity and better mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder, spark plasma sintering, or mechanical alloying that often suffer from phase separation and voids.
generation.boundary: The intervention is valid for powder-based (or skeleton) W–Cu composites processed at sub-melting Cu temperatures. Its efficacy must be maintained under service conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints (high thermal gradients and irradiation).
generation.uncertainty: While vapor deposition has been shown to yield near‐perfect contact in W powders, the exact magnitude of thermal and mechanical improvements, especially under prolonged irradiation, remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples using identical W particle feedstock. One set receives a pre-sinter vapor coating of Cu via CVD or PVD before consolidation by spark plasma sintering. The control set is fabricated under identical SPS conditions without the vapor coating. Subject both sets to simulated fusion reactor service conditions including high thermal flux and neutron irradiation.
measurements: Interfacial quality (void content and bonding) via high-resolution electron microscopy.
Thermal conductivity measurements under elevated temperatures.
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., microhardness, tensile strength) before and after irradiation.
Irradiation-induced defect accumulation monitored by appropriate spectroscopic or diffraction techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vapor-coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity, thermal transport properties, and mechanical durability compared to the control samples under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This manuscript shows the study of the structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of high-entropy borides MeB2 (Me = Ti, Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr). High-entropy borides were synthesized by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h. The structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of the resulting high-entropy borides have been studied. A single-phase hexagonal structure is formed during spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders at 2000 °C. The microhardness of the samples ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV. Gas-dynamic tests of the synthesized materials showed that an increase in the content of Zr and Hf in the composition increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the material.

CrMnFeCoNi alloy can be fabricated by either casting (melting and solidification) [,,,], sintering (powder metallurgy) [,,,], or other methods [,,,,]. Compared with the more frequently studied casting, sintering has a great economic advantage in saving materials and energy []. On the other hand, the element distribution in sintered alloys is usually more inhomogeneous than that of casted ones. One example is the Cr, Mn, and O enrichment in spark-plasma-sintered alloys []. The zones with specific element enrichment generally affect the mechanical properties and electrochemical stability. In addition, the impurities of carbon or oxygen from raw powders also play essential roles in the above properties. Therefore, the relationship between the specific microstructure, the mechanical properties, and the electrochemical stability of sintered alloys needs to be sufficiently clarified. Until now, many CrMnFeCoNi alloys have been sintered under specific conditions, and their mechanical properties have been studied [,,,,,,].
